title: Seven conditions of welfare
hookLine: the last journey begins: a people thrives while it meets often and in harmony

cards: A king wants a war. Ajatasattu of Magadha, the same king who rode out on a moonlit night a few weeks back on this path, has decided to crush the Vajjians, a confederation of clans to the north.

Before he marches, he sends his chief minister, Vassakara, to the Buddha on Vulture's Peak, with orders: tell him my plan, and bring back exactly what he says. For, the king says, a Buddha does not speak falsely.
So the minister arrives, bows, and lays out the plan. And the Buddha doesn't answer him. He turns to Ananda, who is standing behind him, fanning him.

teach.b: The discourse is the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the great discourse on the final passing, the account of the Buddha's last months. Maha means great. Parinibbana is the complete going out, the death of one already awakened.
It begins, of all places, with politics. Ananda, the Buddha asks, have you heard that the Vajjians meet often, and in large numbers? I have, sir.
Then, as long as they do, they can be expected to grow, not decline.
And he goes through seven questions. Do they meet in harmony, rise in harmony, and do their business in harmony? Do they keep their established laws, neither making new ones nor throwing out the old?
Do they honor and listen to their elders? Do they refrain from carrying off women and girls by force? Do they honor their shrines?
Do they protect those who live the holy life among them? Seven yeses, seven reasons to thrive. The minister gets the message.
The Vajjians, he says, can't be beaten in war, only by diplomacy or by splitting them apart. And he goes.

teach.h: THE SAME SEVEN FOR THE MONKS.
teach.b: Then the Buddha calls the monks together and gives them seven conditions of their own, starting the same way: as long as you meet often, and in harmony, you can be expected to grow, not decline. Look at what comes first.
People who keep showing up, and who leave on good terms. The Buddha's great final journey opens with a lesson about how communities stay alive.

how: Buddhist monastic communities meet regularly, most visibly at the fortnightly uposatha gathering where the monastic rules are recited, and many lay groups keep weekly sittings and study meetings.

o: the great war between Magadha and the Vajjians
the great final passing of the Buddha
a great council called to settle disputes

p: the minister sent to the Buddha
the final passing of one awakened

s: the Mahaparinibbana Sutta opens with a question about war
King Ajatasattu sends his minister to ask about attacking the Vajjians.
the Buddha answers the minister directly
he turns to Ananda and asks him seven questions about the Vajjians.
the first condition for the monks is about meditation
it is meeting often, and in harmony.

games.q: you're the king's minister. you've heard seven reasons the Vajjians will thrive. what do you report?
o: that they can be beaten easily.
that they can't be beaten in war, only by diplomacy or by splitting them.
that the Buddha refused to answer.
games.why: Vassakara concludes the Vajjians can't be conquered by war while they keep the seven, only by diplomacy or dividing them.

practice: Call to mind the people you belong with, a family, a team, friends, a congregation, and picture the last time you were all together.
Let one face come up whom you haven't seen in a while, breathe with it, and hold one wish for the group: may we keep meeting, in harmony.

wordCard.voice: Mahaparinibbana. The great final passing, the name of the Long Discourse that tells the Buddha's last journey. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali mahaparinibbana: maha, great; parinibbana, the complete passing of an awakened one.

carryVoice: Your line: meet often, in harmony. Showing up, and leaving on good terms, comes first. That's day five hundred forty-five.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), opening: Vassakara and the seven conditions of welfare
